law: A step is done when it has a link. The spine is the six gates, the mission and the Career core. Publish waits for a receipt.

nodes.title: Welcome
nodes.evidence: A short public note (gist or Google Doc) with two things: the board rule in your own words, and which two open steps you will work on this week.
nodes.why: Write one short note. That is the whole first step.
nodes.reading: This page is the written lesson.
nodes.reviewFor: the rule said plainly, with no appeal to effort or hours, plus two steps that can run in the same week because nothing connects them on the map.

tasks.title: Write the rule in your own words
tasks.done_when: Your note has one or two sentences, in your words, explaining when a step lights and why that rule exists.
how: Open a gist or a Google Doc. Write the rule the way you would explain it to a friend.
If your sentence mentions effort or time spent, rewrite it. Keep both answers in the same note.

tasks.title: Name two steps you can run this week
tasks.done_when: The same note names It runs and The four skills (or any two open steps with no line between them), plus one sentence on how you will split the week.
how: Default pair while both are open: It runs (get a system running on your machine) and The four skills (write the skill names with examples). Look at the map: no connecting line means they are independent.
One URL lights this step. Paste it under Turn this in when you are ready.

proves.claim: You can state the one rule the board runs on and pick two steps that can run in the same week.
proves.challenge: Write the rule in your own words and name two open steps with no line between them.
proves.evidence: One short public note.
proves.falsification: A rule that appeals to hours or effort instead of a link; two steps that depend on each other.
proves.threshold: The rule said plainly, two independent steps named.
proves.transfer: Every later step ends with a link, and every Monday you name what runs in parallel.

nodes.title: How a working week runs
nodes.evidence: A short public note that states the loop in your own words (story, branch, PR, review, merge) and links your merged onboarding PR.
nodes.why: Real teams run on a board of small user stories, not one big assignment. This chapter installs the loop you will run every week from here on: pick a story, branch, open a PR, take the review, merge.
nodes.reading: Everything is on this page. The ticket board, Discord, and the repos are linked from Calendar and the map list.
nodes.reviewFor: the loop said plainly in your words, and one real PR, however small, that went through review and merged.

tasks.title: Read the ticket board
tasks.done_when: You can name the story you would take first and say why it is the right size.
how: Open the board and read every story in the ready column. Each one carries a size and a done-when.
Small and finished beats ambitious and half-done. That rule never changes here.

tasks.title: Run one full loop, small on purpose
tasks.done_when: Your onboarding PR (adding yourself to the contributors file) is open, reviewed, and merged.
how: Branch off main, make the one-line change, push, open the PR, and ask for a review in #asks naming what to check.
If you have never done this, the film above walks every click. Nobody here assumes you have.

tasks.title: Save the note and the PR
tasks.done_when: One public note links your merged PR and states the loop in your own words.
how: A gist or a doc works. That URL is what you turn in below.

video.title: The weekly loop: stories, branches, reviews

proves.claim: You can run the weekly loop, story to branch to PR to review to merge, and say which work state a ticket is honestly in.
proves.challenge: Take a trivial story through the full ceremony and state the loop in your own words.
proves.evidence: A public note with the loop and the merged onboarding PR.
proves.falsification: A PR that skipped review; a status given as a column instead of a state.
proves.threshold: One merged PR through review, the loop stated plainly.
proves.transfer: Every ticket from Your first ticket on runs this loop; Monday status names a state.

nodes.title: It runs
nodes.evidence: a gist with the outputs of the onboarding doc's current verification steps, plus a screenshot of your avatar standing in your locally-running world.
nodes.why: Before you can change a live system you must be able to run it: the same code, started the same way production starts it, on your own machine.
nodes.reading: ONBOARDING.md in the world server repo is the living setup doc. It always reflects the world's current state; when the world changes, it changes. Follow the live doc.
nodes.reviewFor: Both boot paths ran, and you can say what is different about them.

tasks.title: Run the world server, both ways
tasks.done_when: The server runs in dev mode AND under Docker, and you completed every verification step the onboarding doc currently lists.
how: ONBOARDING.md walks it command by command. If a step fails, the error is the lesson; 30 honest minutes, then #asks.

tasks.title: Compare dev mode to production mode
tasks.done_when: Your gist shows the same endpoint answering in both modes, with one sentence on why any difference exists.
how: The difference, or its absence, is the week-1 systems lesson.

tasks.title: Walk into your own world
tasks.done_when: A public image or gist shows two browser tabs, two avatars, on your local world. That URL is the evidence.
how: Point the web client at your local server; the onboarding doc shows how.
Screenshot both tabs, upload to a gist or image host, paste the link.

video.title: A live game server on your laptop

proves.claim: You can run the production system on your own machine both ways it runs in production, and explain any difference.
proves.challenge: Boot the world server in dev mode and under Docker; complete every verification step; compare one endpoint across both.
proves.evidence: A gist of the verification outputs and a screenshot of two avatars in your local world.
proves.falsification: Only one boot path works; a difference between modes you cannot explain.
proves.threshold: Both paths run, verification steps complete, one sentence on the difference.
proves.transfer: Every ticket starts from a running local world; Staging to live asks you to reason about the same two modes at deploy time.

nodes.title: The four skills
nodes.evidence: A one-page note: the four skills in your words, with one honest example each from work you have already done.
nodes.why: Every review here uses four named skills. Learn the names calmly now, before a review uses them about your work.
nodes.reading: The four are explained below. Your evidence is the four skills in your own words.
nodes.reviewFor: each skill in your words, plus one example from work you have already done, including a time you lacked the skill.

tasks.title: Write the four in your words
tasks.done_when: Each skill has one sentence and one example from your work.
how: Template: for each skill, one sentence in your words, then one example from work you have already done. Include at least one miss.

tasks.title: Save the note
tasks.done_when: Anyone can open the link (gist or doc) and read all four skills with your examples.
how: Paste a public gist or doc URL, somewhere a stranger can read the text.

proves.claim: You can name the four skills in your own words and recognise each in work you have already done, including where you lacked it.
proves.challenge: Write one page: each skill, one sentence, one honest example.
proves.evidence: The one-page note at a public URL.
proves.falsification: Definitions copied rather than owned; examples that are all flattering; no example of lacking a skill.
proves.threshold: Four sentences in your words, four examples, at least one a miss.
proves.transfer: The defense in week 7 asks these four, one by one; every review reply uses their names.

modules.title: 00 · The engineer this program is building

nodes.title: You can read a system
nodes.evidence: A note that traces one real path through the world server, a player connects and everyone sees them move, and names three files a change would break.
nodes.why: The job is inherited systems: code that existed before you arrived. If you cannot redraw a path from memory, you have not understood it yet.
nodes.reading: The world server repo is the system. This lesson explains the tracing method.
nodes.reviewFor: a map drawn before any assistant, naming three files a change would break.

tasks.title: Trace one player's movement
tasks.done_when: You can redraw the path from memory, a browser connects, the server assigns identity, position updates arrive, the loop broadcasts to everyone, without the code open.
how: Read in the data's order, not the file order. Start where a note enters the system and follow the calls. Paper beats screen here; redrawing is a test of memory, not art.

tasks.title: Save the trace
tasks.done_when: A public note or gist names the path, the trust boundary you found on it, and three files a change would touch.
how: One URL. Paper photo is fine if the writing is readable.

video.title: Reading code you did not write

proves.claim: You can enter a system you did not write and produce a model that predicts its behaviour, and you can say which parts you are unsure of.
proves.challenge: Trace one real path through the world server without an assistant; redraw it from memory; answer counterfactuals before checking.
proves.evidence: A public note with the path, the trust boundary you found, three files a change would touch, and your counterfactual answers with confidence.
proves.falsification: A fluent summary that cannot answer 'what happens if'; a map drawn after asking an assistant; claims with no confidence attached.
proves.threshold: Redrawn from memory; most counterfactual predictions right; the ones you were unsure of marked as such.
proves.transfer: Every ticket's map-before-you-touch; the changed-fact question in You defend it live; modelling your own system in You modeled it before you built it.

nodes.title: You found the real problem
nodes.evidence: A public framing note for one real problem in the world: observation, symptom, at least three hypotheses, the evidence you gathered, the cause you believe with a confidence, the opportunity, the smallest intervention, and what you set aside.
nodes.why: Most wasted engineering starts by fixing the first thing that came to mind. Before your first ticket you prove you can walk from what a player saw to what is actually wrong, and stop before the code.
nodes.reading: Read Problem framing (disciplines 03) first. Pick from the world's open issues, the #bugs channel, or something you saw yourself in It runs. No changes to the code on this step; reading and logs are allowed.
nodes.reviewFor: more than one hypothesis, evidence that separates them, a cause with a stated confidence, a 'not doing' row, and no code.

tasks.title: Pick one observation
tasks.done_when: One sentence you could show a stranger and they would agree it happened, with where and when you saw it.
how: Sources: the world's issue list, #bugs, your own session in It runs. An observation is a fact. 'Movement feels bad' is a symptom and goes in the next row.

tasks.title: Write three hypotheses and the evidence for each
tasks.done_when: At least three competing explanations, each with the single cheapest piece of evidence that would raise or lower your confidence in it.
how: If you can only think of one, ask the Coach for two more and then argue with them.
Do not open the editor to fix anything. Reading code and logs is allowed; changing them is not.

tasks.title: Gather the evidence and pick the cause
tasks.done_when: You looked at the evidence for at least two hypotheses and named the surviving cause with a confidence percentage.
how: Logs, a reproduction, the code path you traced in You can read a system, a question to a player. Write what you found next to each hypothesis, including the ones it killed.

tasks.title: Save the framing note
tasks.done_when: One public URL with all eight rows: observation, symptom, hypotheses, evidence, cause, opportunity, intervention, not doing.
how: Gist or doc. The 'not doing' row is where most of the judgment shows.

proves.claim: You can walk from an observation to a proposed intervention without skipping a link, and you stop before the code.
proves.challenge: Given one real problem in the world and no instruction about what is wrong, produce a framing with competing hypotheses and the evidence that separates them.
proves.evidence: The framing note at a public URL, eight rows.
proves.falsification: One hypothesis only; a cause chosen before any evidence was looked at; a diff opened before the note existed.
proves.threshold: Three or more hypotheses, evidence gathered for at least two, a cause with a confidence, and a 'not doing' row.
proves.transfer: Every later ticket's contract opens with this chain in one paragraph. A number moved runs it against a metric instead of a bug.

nodes.title: Someone else can build it
nodes.evidence: A specification for the story you will take on Your first ticket: functional requirement, invariants, non-functional requirements, given-when-then acceptance criteria, unknowns, out of scope, plus the clarification count from a handoff test you did not talk through.
nodes.why: A vague ticket used to waste one engineer's afternoon. Handed to agents it produces confident wrongness at scale. Before you execute anything you prove your words can be executed by someone who cannot ask you.
nodes.reading: Read Specification engineering (disciplines 04). Specify the story you framed in You found the real problem, or the story you will take from the board on Monday. Its accepted version becomes the contract on your first PR.
nodes.reviewFor: acceptance criteria a test could be written from, invariants stated as checkable sentences, a real unknowns list, and a clarification count from a handoff you did not talk through.

tasks.title: Write the six parts
tasks.done_when: Functional requirement, invariants, non-functional requirements, acceptance criteria as given-when-then, unknowns, out of scope: each present and each specific to this story.
how: Write the invariants before the requirement if you can. The requirement often changes once you see what it must not break.
An empty unknowns section means you did not look.

tasks.title: Run the handoff test
tasks.done_when: A cohortmate or an agent, given only the document, listed every decision it would have to make that the document does not settle. You recorded the count.
how: Agent version: paste the spec and ask for the list of unsettled decisions, with the instruction not to implement anything.
Human version: post in #asks, ask for questions only, and do not answer until they are all in.

tasks.title: Revise until the list is short
tasks.done_when: The unsettled-decision list is at two or fewer, or the remainder is honestly moved into Unknowns. Both counts, before and after, are in the note.
how: Every 'I would assume' from the reader becomes a requirement or an unknown. Assumptions that stay in your head are the ones that get executed wrong.

tasks.title: Save the spec
tasks.done_when: One public URL with the spec and both clarification counts.
how: Gist or doc. This document rides on your first PR as the contract.

proves.claim: You can turn a framed problem into a contract another person or an agent executes without asking you.
proves.challenge: Specify a real story, hand it to someone who cannot reach you, and count what they had to ask.
proves.evidence: The spec at a public URL, with before and after clarification counts.
proves.falsification: Acceptance criteria no test could be written from; an empty unknowns list; a clarification count that was never measured.
proves.threshold: Two or fewer unsettled decisions after revision, invariants as checkable sentences, unknowns named.
proves.transfer: The accepted contract on every PR from Your first ticket on. The handoff repeats in Someone else marked it up, where a reviewer executes your reasoning instead of your spec.

nodes.title: Source code is data
nodes.evidence: a repo where nanograph parses itself, plus graph.json generated from a real project you did not write.
nodes.why: Comprehension made executable. Every question you will ever ask about a codebase, who calls this, what breaks, starts with the graph you build here.
nodes.reading: Three text modules. Type the code. Do not paste it.
nodes.reviewFor: nanograph.py parses itself, the nested-function bug is fixed, and graph.json exists for a repo you did not write.

tasks.title: Modules 00-01: the parser parses itself
tasks.done_when: nanograph.py reports its own functions and calls, and you fixed the nested-function bug from the exercise.
how: Python stdlib ast. Nothing to install.

tasks.title: Module 02: edges across files
tasks.done_when: graph.json exists for a real repo, and you committed the ambiguity confession from the exercise.
how: Two passes: collect definitions, then resolve calls.

proves.claim: You can turn source code into a graph you own, and run it on code you did not write.
proves.challenge: Build the parser until it parses itself; generate graph.json for a foreign repo.
proves.evidence: The repo and graph.json.
proves.falsification: The parser cannot parse itself; the nested-function bug is still there; only your own code was graphed.
proves.threshold: Self-parse works, nested functions fixed, one foreign repo graphed.
proves.transfer: Every later graph module; mapping the world server in Swap the parser, keep the graph.

nodes.title: Who calls what
nodes.evidence: CLI output of callers, callees, and a --hops blast radius on a repo you care about, committed to the README.
nodes.why: “If I change this, what breaks?” answered in milliseconds instead of an afternoon. This is the question interviews actually probe.
nodes.reading: Modules 03-04. Type the code. One dial: --hops.
nodes.reviewFor: callers, callees, and a --hops blast radius on a repo you care about, in the README.

tasks.title: callers / callees commands
tasks.done_when: nanograph callers <fn> answers from graph.json without re-parsing.
how: Build the reverse index once; queries are lookups.

tasks.title: Blast radius with --hops
tasks.done_when: Reverse BFS matches the paper drawing you made in module 00, or you can explain the difference.
how: Your hand-drawn graph from episode 00 is the test fixture.

proves.claim: You can answer 'if I change this, what breaks' in milliseconds, with the evidence tier of each hit.
proves.challenge: Implement callers, callees and a hops-bounded blast radius; run them on a repo you care about.
proves.evidence: CLI output in the README.
proves.falsification: Blast radius with no depth bound; hits with no idea where the edge came from; a toy repo only.
proves.threshold: Three commands, run on a real repo, output committed.
proves.transfer: Map before you touch on every ticket; the boundary table in You ran the agents.

nodes.title: Your first ticket
nodes.evidence: A merged pull request from the ticket board, carrying your engineering contract, failure log, and agent log.
nodes.why: The center of the program: real changes to a live system, taken from the board as user stories and shipped with professional ceremony. This step lights on your first. The ones after it come weekly.
nodes.reading: Your story comes from the ticket board in Monday planning, or message Aden when you are ready and you will have one the same day. This lesson explains the ceremony.
nodes.reviewFor: a story of the right size, a contract accepted before the diff, and both logs riding with the merged PR.

tasks.title: Take a story in planning
tasks.done_when: A story from the board is assigned to you, with its size and done-when read aloud in the Monday call.
how: Pick small. One finished small story with full ceremony beats a half-done ambitious one every time.
Stories default to the world. GridSeak stories sit on the same board for anyone whose goals want the harder systems work.

tasks.title: Map before you touch
tasks.done_when: A written half-page: what the story touches, what calls that code, what could break downstream.
how: The tracing method from You can read a system, applied to your story's corner of the code.

tasks.title: Write the contract, then ship the PR
tasks.done_when: Your PR is open with the accepted contract, the failure log, and the agent log riding in it, review requested, CI green.
how: The contract is the spec you wrote in Someone else can build it, accepted in planning. Code second. Do not tidy the repo to make the story prettier.
Name the work state in the PR description as it moves: specified, agent executing, evaluating, needs human judgment.

tasks.title: Settle your predictions
tasks.done_when: Next to each counterfactual you wrote in You can read a system, one line: confirmed, wrong, or untested, with the evidence. The count of wrong ones is written at the top.

tasks.title: Save the merged PR
tasks.done_when: The URL is the merged PR.
how: Submit it.

video.title: Working inside code you did not write

proves.claim: You can take a story of the right size through a live team's ceremony: contract accepted before the diff, PR with both logs, review, merge.
proves.challenge: Take one small story from the board and ship it with full ceremony while a second thread stays open.
proves.evidence: The merged PR, carrying the contract, the failure log and the agent log.
proves.falsification: Contract written after the code; a trap story taken; logs missing or flattering; a diff that touched what the contract said it would not.
proves.threshold: Right size, contract accepted before the diff, both logs honest, merged after review.
proves.transfer: You ship on a cadence repeats it twice more; the defense picks the strongest of these PRs.

nodes.title: You can prove it
nodes.evidence: A check that fails before your change and passes after it, runnable by a stranger from your link.
nodes.why: A test that exists is different from a check that would catch a real lie. Every story you ship carries one, and this step is where you prove you can write it.
nodes.reading: Write it for the story you shipped in Your first ticket. Optional brief: Verification tax.
nodes.reviewFor: a check that fails while the bug is present, passes after your fix, and runs for a stranger.

tasks.title: Write the stranger-runnable check
tasks.done_when: One command anyone can run. You watched it fail before your change and pass after.
how: Do not delete the old tests. Add the one that tells the truth beside them.

tasks.title: Find the defect the green suite missed
tasks.done_when: You picked one audited world bug whose existing tests pass, wrote the check that fails on main because of it, and recorded which of the passing tests should have caught it and why it did not.

tasks.title: Save the check
tasks.done_when: The link is the test file on your PR or the command output.
how: Repo file on the PR.

proves.claim: You can write a check that would catch a real defect, and you can name the result that would have made you revert.
proves.challenge: Write one stranger-runnable check for your story; watch it fail before the fix and pass after; then find a real defect an existing green suite lets through.
proves.evidence: The check on the PR or its command output, runnable by a stranger.
proves.falsification: A check that passes before the fix too; a check that needs you standing next to it; no attempt to break the change; trusting green because it is green.
proves.threshold: Fails while the defect is present, passes after, one command, and a sentence on what you tried to break.
proves.transfer: Every later PR carries one; the evaluation harness in Someone else can use it; the measurement in A number moved.

nodes.title: You ran the agents
nodes.evidence: An execution record for one ticket: the decomposition, what was delegated and what you kept, the boundary table, every intervention with its cause named, cost and elapsed time, and one measured comparison of one task run with one agent and with several.
nodes.why: Using an assistant is not the skill. Directing machine work so a reviewer can see what the human contributed is, and it is the question employers are starting to ask and cannot yet answer.
nodes.reading: Read Agentic workflow engineering (disciplines 05). The record covers your first ticket or the next one; the agent log already riding on your PR is the raw material. Cost and time are requirements whether or not anyone wrote them down.
nodes.reviewFor: a decomposition with context per task, a boundary table, every intervention logged with its cause named (spec, agent, or you), cost and time recorded, one comparison actually run.

tasks.title: Decompose and set the boundaries
tasks.done_when: No more than six tasks, each with the context it needs, what it could break, and how you will know it is done; plus a table of what the machine may do alone and where it must stop and ask.
how: A task that cannot be rejected on its own is too large. The whole repository is never the context.
Serial is the honest default. Parallelise only the pairs you can show are independent.

tasks.title: Execute with the record open
tasks.done_when: The ticket's work is done with an assistant or agents, and every intervention is one line in the record: what it did, why you stopped it, what you changed.
how: Record the embarrassing ones. Seventeen honest interventions is evidence; two claimed ones is not.
Note tokens or dollars and wall-clock time at the end. An expensive right answer failed a requirement.

tasks.title: Compare one task, one agent against several
tasks.done_when: One task from the decomposition run both ways, with completion, correctness, interventions, cost and time side by side, and one sentence on what you would do next time.
how: The cheapest sufficient tool is the finding. Sometimes it is you, typing, for eleven minutes.

tasks.title: Save the record
tasks.done_when: One public URL with the record. Link it from the PR too.
how: Gist, doc, or a file on the PR.

proves.claim: You can direct machine work and produce a record from which a stranger reconstructs what the human did.
proves.challenge: Run a real ticket with agents; log every intervention with its cause; compare one task run two ways on cost, time and correctness.
proves.evidence: The execution record at a public URL, linked from the PR.
proves.falsification: A record with no interventions on non-trivial work; cost or time missing; a comparison described but never run.
proves.threshold: Every intervention logged with its cause named; cost and time present; one measured comparison with a next-time sentence.
proves.transfer: The agent log on every later PR. The cost line in your defense. The orchestration of your own system in Someone else can use it.

nodes.title: LinkedIn that reads as you
nodes.evidence: Your LinkedIn profile URL, after Aden left written feedback and you applied the notes that matter.
nodes.why: Hiring is a risk calculation, and your profile is usually the first place a stranger decides whether working with you looks predictable enough to keep reading.
nodes.reading: Rewrite Headline and About with the templates below, feature one proof URL, get Aden's written review, apply the notes that matter, and submit the live profile URL.
nodes.reviewFor: Headline searchable and specific. About readable in three short blocks with one concrete receipt. Featured leads with one real proof URL, not tutorials. Aden's notes applied or answered.

tasks.title: Rewrite Headline and About
tasks.done_when: Headline is searchable and specific. About has three short blocks and one concrete receipt.
how: Use the templates in the lesson. No passionate about code. Point at mission work when you have it.

tasks.title: Feature one proof URL
tasks.done_when: Featured (or the top Experience lines) opens one real receipt: PR, project page, or demo.
how: Prefer the mission PR or project page. Demote tutorial clones.

tasks.title: Get Aden's written feedback
tasks.done_when: Aden left notes on the profile in a review thread or doc you can link.
how: Post the profile URL in #asks with Career · LinkedIn review.

tasks.title: Save the live profile URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the updated public profile.
how: Submit the public LinkedIn URL after the notes that matter are applied.

proves.claim: A stranger reading your profile can tell in one screen what you do and find one real receipt.
proves.challenge: Rewrite Headline and About; feature one proof URL; take written feedback and apply what matters.
proves.evidence: The live profile URL after feedback was applied.
proves.falsification: A headline that could be anyone's; Featured leading with a tutorial; notes ignored without a reason.
proves.threshold: Searchable headline, three-block About with one receipt, Featured leads with real proof, notes applied or answered.
proves.transfer: A stranger can find the work points here at the end; every post from the content system lands on this profile.

nodes.title: Your look, on every screen
nodes.evidence: A public design-system note (tokens, type, one accent, spacing, a diagram theme, a screenshot convention), agreed with Aden in a design session, and one diagram from your work rendered in your theme. Every later surface you publish is checked against it.
nodes.why: Everything you put in public should look like one person with a method made it. Consistency is read as competence before a word is read; inconsistency is read as the opposite.
nodes.reading: Read The portfolio thread (disciplines 11), the design system section. The method is the one this program used for its own site: write the tokens once, apply them everywhere, hand the note to an assistant with 'apply this' and check the output against it.
nodes.reviewFor: tokens written as variables rather than remembered, one diagram theme file actually used, and three artifacts a stranger would guess came from the same person.

tasks.title: Write the tokens
tasks.done_when: One file: two or three colours and one accent, a prose face and a code face, a heading scale and a body size that read at phone width, a spacing scale. Variables, not adjectives.
how: Small is a feature. If you cannot hold the whole system in one screen, it is not a system yet.

tasks.title: Design session with Aden
tasks.done_when: You walked Aden through the tokens in a 1:1 and the note records the two choices you argued about and what you decided.

tasks.title: Make the diagram theme
tasks.done_when: A Mermaid theme configuration using your tokens, and one diagram from your work rendered with it.
how: The diagrams in the disciplines readings are this program's theme. Yours should be recognisably not that.

tasks.title: Save the design-system note
tasks.done_when: One public URL with the note, the two session decisions, and the rendered diagram.
how: A page on your own site is the natural home.

proves.claim: You can define a personal design system once, defend its choices, and hold every surface you publish to it.
proves.challenge: Write tokens and a diagram theme; argue them through with Aden in one design session; render one real diagram in the theme.
proves.evidence: The design-system note, with the session's two decisions recorded, and the rendered diagram.
proves.falsification: Tokens that exist only in your head; a theme file never rendered; a note with no decision anyone argued about.
proves.threshold: One-screen token file, one rendered themed diagram, the two session decisions written down. The site, project pages and defense visual are checked against it at their own steps.
proves.transfer: Your site is live applies it; The work is on the site and every project page, post, research write-up and defense visual are read against it.

nodes.title: You modeled it before you built it
nodes.evidence: A public model note for a system you will own: the archetype and domain, the domain model, the boundary between what a model decides and what deterministic code enforces, the invariants, where a human is escalated to, and the spec for the first version.
nodes.why: Your tickets test whether you can change a system someone else owns. Your own system tests whether you can create one, and its first artifact is a model, not code.
nodes.reading: The archetype is fixed: a system that observes changing information, makes a decision, takes an action, and proves whether the action worked. You choose the domain. Read System comprehension (01), Specification engineering (04) and The portfolio thread (11) before you write a line.
nodes.reviewFor: a real fit to the archetype, a drawn boundary between probabilistic and deterministic parts, invariants as checkable sentences, an escalation boundary, and a first-version spec that would pass the handoff test.

tasks.title: Choose the domain inside the archetype
tasks.done_when: One paragraph: what it observes, what it decides, what action it takes, how it proves the action worked, and who outside you would use it.
how: Shapes that fit: a support agent that reads tickets, classifies, retrieves, proposes, escalates and measures resolution. A research system that tracks sources, extracts claims, keeps provenance and flags contradictions. A finance analyser that imports, categorises, flags anomalies and measures savings. A developer agent that takes an issue to an evaluated PR. A game intelligence that observes state, acts and learns.
Pick something you would want even if nobody graded it. You will live with it for five weeks.

tasks.title: Draw the model
tasks.done_when: State and who owns it, the event flow, the line between what the model decides and what code enforces, at least three invariants as testable sentences, and the exact point where a human is escalated to.
how: Mermaid or paper. The value is in the labels on the arrows and the sentence under it that says who owns the truth.

tasks.title: Specify the first version
tasks.done_when: The six parts from Someone else can build it, for the smallest version that meets the ten requirements in Someone else can use it, with a handoff count.
how: Out of scope will be your longest section. That is correct for a first version.

tasks.title: Save the model note
tasks.done_when: One public URL with archetype, model, invariants, escalation boundary and spec.
how: Gist, doc, or a page on your site.

proves.claim: You can model a system you intend to build, including where machine judgment stops and deterministic code begins.
proves.challenge: Choose a domain inside the archetype; produce model, invariants, escalation boundary, and a first-version spec.
proves.evidence: The model note at a public URL.
proves.falsification: No deterministic component; no escalation boundary; invariants missing or untestable; a spec that fails the handoff test.
proves.threshold: Every element present and specific to the domain; spec handoff count at two or fewer.
proves.transfer: Someone else can use it builds from this. If you choose your own system for the defense, the model is what you defend.

nodes.title: Cycles, rank, coupling
nodes.evidence: a findings write-up with numbers: one real cycle, the top five load-bearing functions, the worst-coupled module pair.
nodes.why: Architecture stops being an opinion when you can measure it. PageRank on a call graph finds the code everyone leans on.
nodes.reading: Modules 05-07. PageRank is repeated averaging; no math beyond fractions.
nodes.reviewFor: A findings write-up that reads like a review comment, not a data dump.

tasks.title: Find real cycles
tasks.done_when: nanograph cycles names at least one true cycle in a real repo, and you explain why it matters or doesn't.
how: DFS with a stack. Module 05 walks it.

tasks.title: Rank + coupling with numbers
tasks.done_when: A note or PR comment in your nanograph repo ranks load-bearing symbols with numbers, in code-review tone, not a raw dump.
how: Degree first, then PageRank. Modules 06-07 open under this step.
Commit the write-up next to graph.json, or paste a gist URL that quotes the numbers.

proves.claim: You can measure architecture instead of having opinions about it.
proves.challenge: Find one real cycle, rank load-bearing functions, name the worst-coupled module pair, with numbers.
proves.evidence: A findings write-up.
proves.falsification: A data dump instead of findings; a cycle that is not real; numbers with no reading of what they mean.
proves.threshold: One real cycle, top five by rank, worst pair, each with a sentence a reviewer would write.
proves.transfer: The review comments you leave on peers' PRs; structural claims in your defense.

nodes.title: You ship on a cadence
nodes.evidence: Two more merged pull requests from the ticket board, each with full ceremony, linked from one note.
nodes.why: One merged PR proves you can. A cadence of them proves you would on a team. This is the difference between a project and a track record.
nodes.reading: Same board, same loop. Pick in Monday planning, or message Aden when you are free.
nodes.reviewFor: two more merged stories, each mapped before touched, each with contract and logs, at the size you promised in planning.

tasks.title: Ship two more stories
tasks.done_when: Both PRs are merged with full ceremony, and your size estimates were said out loud in the Monday call.
how: Estimate before you start and say the number in planning. Hitting a modest estimate beats blowing past an ambitious one.
If your nanograph already parses this repo's language (graph track, seam node), use it for the map step. That is why you are building it.

tasks.title: Save the PRs
tasks.done_when: One public note links both merged PRs.
how: A gist works. Submit that URL.

proves.claim: You can ship on a team more than once: the same ceremony, at the size you promised, twice more.
proves.challenge: Ship two more stories from the board with full ceremony.
proves.evidence: Two more merged PRs linked from one note.
proves.falsification: Stories that grew past their planned size; a PR without contract or logs; a failure met and not written down.
proves.threshold: Two merged, each mapped before touched, each with contract and logs, at planned size.
proves.transfer: The cadence you keep in the arena; the failure notes feed your defense.

nodes.title: Your site is live
nodes.evidence: A public URL for your personal site that loads without a local server.
nodes.why: A public URL is the home for your work: the link on LinkedIn and a resume, and the place a stranger can answer who you are, where proof will live, and how to reach you without cloning your laptop.
nodes.reading: Ship one public HTTPS page with who you are, where projects will live, and how to reach you, then wire LinkedIn both ways. Localhost does not count.
nodes.reviewFor: Loads over HTTPS for a stranger. Who you are is clear above the fold. Contact plus LinkedIn and GitHub are findable without hunting. A projects section or placeholder exists for The work is on the site. Dead links fail.

tasks.title: Ship a one-page home
tasks.done_when: The page says who you are for, points to where work will live, shows how to reach you, and uses your tokens from Your look, on every screen.
how: Match the tone of your LinkedIn Headline and About. One honest page beats a half-finished redesign.

tasks.title: Host it on a public HTTPS URL
tasks.done_when: A public HTTPS URL serves the page without a local server.
how: GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, or equivalent. Custom domain is optional.

tasks.title: Wire the same URL into LinkedIn
tasks.done_when: LinkedIn About, Featured, or Contact includes the live site URL, and the site links back to LinkedIn and GitHub.
how: One story across surfaces. Do not leave the new URL orphaned.

tasks.title: Save the live URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the site from a private window.
how: Submit the public site URL.

proves.claim: You can put a public HTTPS page live that says who you are, where proof will live, and how to reach you.
proves.challenge: Ship a one-page home on a public URL and wire LinkedIn both ways.
proves.evidence: The live URL, loading without a local server.
proves.falsification: Localhost; a page that does not say who you are above the fold; dead links.
proves.threshold: Loads over HTTPS for a stranger, identity clear, contact and links findable, projects placeholder exists.
proves.transfer: The work is on the site builds on this page; every project page and research post lives here, in the look you defined.

nodes.title: Someone else marked it up
nodes.evidence: The review thread URL, showing another person marked up the work.
nodes.why: Solo work is unverified work. Reviews here are weekly, up to three pieces of work each week, and this step lights on your first real thread.
nodes.reading: The request format is in the lesson. Reviews run weekly through #asks and your board; send work that is ready to be inspected.
nodes.reviewFor: how you asked, and how you answered: selective agreement, not a blanket yes.

tasks.title: Ask for the review properly
tasks.done_when: The request names what to look at and what you are unsure about.
how: Template: look at <file or lines> · I am unsure about <risk>. Do not make them find the risk.

tasks.title: Save the thread
tasks.done_when: The thread shows another person's marks.
how: Submit the URL.

video.title: Send work, get notes, change it

proves.claim: You can ask for review like a professional and answer it with selective agreement rather than a blanket yes.
proves.challenge: Request review on real work with your own doubt named; answer every comment.
proves.evidence: The review thread URL.
proves.falsification: A request with no doubt named; comments left unanswered; agreement with everything including the wrong notes.
proves.threshold: Doubt named up front, every comment answered, at least one respectful disagreement with a reason.
proves.transfer: Every later PR; the adversarial questions in You defend it live; reviewing a peer's change.

nodes.title: Staging to live, your hands on the wheel
nodes.evidence: the deploy run URL you drove, and the health check you watched go green on the real domain.
nodes.why: Most bootcamp grads have never deployed anything anyone uses. You will have promoted a live multiplayer world with your change in it, on camera, with me beside you.
nodes.reading: The Friday promote session. Merge deploys staging automatically; live is a decision, and this week it is yours to execute.
nodes.reviewFor: You drove the promote, and the deploy note a stranger can open says what changed.

tasks.title: Drive the promote
tasks.done_when: Your ticket's image is serving on the world URL and /health answers over TLS.
how: Group session. You share the screen, not me.

tasks.title: Write the deploy note
tasks.done_when: Five lines in #world: what shipped, how you verified, what you'd watch overnight.
how: The note is the habit; ops teams live on these.

proves.claim: You can promote a live system with your change in it, watch it go healthy, and tell a stranger what changed.
proves.challenge: Drive the Friday promote and write the deploy note.
proves.evidence: The deploy run URL and the health check on the real domain.
proves.falsification: Someone else drove; no health check watched; a deploy note that does not say what changed; no idea what to watch tomorrow.
proves.threshold: You drove it, health went green on the real domain, the note says what changed and what to watch.
proves.transfer: A number moved depends on this path; every production system you touch afterward.

nodes.title: Someone else can use it
nodes.evidence: A deployed URL a stranger can use, plus a note that points at each of the ten requirements in the running system: real persistence, external uncertainty, the model component, the deterministic component, observability, evaluation, failure handling, human escalation, deployment, and at least one outside user.
nodes.why: A demo on your laptop is a promise. A system someone else can open, break, and be helped by is a receipt, and building the ten requirements in is how you meet the boundary between probabilistic and deterministic software for real.
nodes.reading: Ten requirements, every one. Read Agentic workflow engineering (05) as you build with agents and Evaluation engineering (06) before you claim anything works. Keep the execution record from You ran the agents running the whole time.
nodes.reviewFor: the ten requirements each pointed at in the running system, a stranger-runnable evaluation, telemetry you can read back, and one predictable failure handled on purpose.

tasks.title: Build the minimum with agents, record kept
tasks.done_when: The first-version spec is implemented, with real persistence, a model component and a deterministic guard, and the execution record shows every intervention.
how: Agents build from the spec in your model note. Where they had to guess, the spec was wrong; fix the spec, not just the code.

tasks.title: Instrument before you claim
tasks.done_when: You can answer 'what happened on the last ten runs' from telemetry alone, without opening the code.
how: A log line per decision with the inputs it saw and the branch it took is enough for a first version.

tasks.title: Build the evaluation harness
tasks.done_when: One command a stranger can run that exercises the invariants from your model, includes at least one adversarial case, and fails when it should.
how: Break it on purpose once and watch the harness catch it. A harness that has never failed has not been tested.

tasks.title: Deploy where a stranger can reach it
tasks.done_when: A public URL, working, with one person outside you having used it and their session visible in your telemetry.
how: Localhost does not count. A single outside user is the difference between a project and a system.

tasks.title: Save the URL and the ten-point note
tasks.done_when: One public URL for the system and one for the note that points at each requirement.
how: The note belongs on your site's project page eventually. A gist is fine now.

proves.claim: You can take a modeled system to a deployment someone else can use, with observability and evaluation built in from the start.
proves.challenge: Ship the first version meeting all ten requirements, with the build record kept.
proves.evidence: The deployed URL and the ten-point note.
proves.falsification: In-memory only; no telemetry; no evaluation harness or one that has never failed; nobody outside you has used it.
proves.threshold: Ten requirements each demonstrated in the running system; one outside session in the telemetry.
proves.transfer: Real people used it. The project page on your site. The system you may choose to defend.

nodes.title: The work is on the site
nodes.evidence: A projects section on your site with one page per receipt you hold: the merged PR, and any owned system, graph tool or outcome note you have lit. Each page links the real receipt and carries one visual that shows the system moving.
nodes.why: The page a stranger opens has to click through to work you can defend, because that same page becomes the card for LinkedIn Featured, warm intros, and the last minutes of an interview.
nodes.reading: Build one project page around mission work using the receipt shape, add one visual proof, and link artifacts a stranger can open.
nodes.reviewFor: One strong page. Wrong, change, verify, and watch next are named. Links open a real PR, check, demo, or defense. At least one visual receipt. A stranger reaches proof in under a minute.

tasks.title: Write the PR page with receipts
tasks.done_when: The page names what was wrong, what you changed, how a stranger checks it, and what you would watch next, with live links.
how: Prefer the mission PR and check. One strong page beats five tutorial cards.

tasks.title: Add one visual receipt
tasks.done_when: The page includes a short demo, gif, recording, or diagram that shows the change or the system moving, not a decorative screenshot.
how: Default is something that moves. A still diagram or before/after result is the fallback.

tasks.title: One page per receipt you hold
tasks.done_when: Every lit project-type node (your owned system, your graph tool, your outcome note) has its own page with the same four sections and a visual, or the section says plainly that it is coming and when.

tasks.title: Save the project page URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens that page from a private window.
how: Submit the public project page URL.

proves.claim: A stranger can reach real proof of your work from your site in under a minute.
proves.challenge: Write one project page per receipt, each with real links and one visual that shows the system moving.
proves.evidence: The public projects section URL, one page per receipt.
proves.falsification: Tutorial demos; links that open nothing checkable; a decorative screenshot instead of a visual receipt; proof more than a minute away.
proves.threshold: Wrong, change, verify, watch-next named on every page; links open real PR, check, demo or defense; one visual receipt per page; nothing you have lit is missing.
proves.transfer: Every later post links here; the research post and the owned-system note join this page.

nodes.title: A system that feeds posts
nodes.evidence: A public doc or gist that holds your content prompts and one week of drafts produced by that system.
nodes.why: A small engine turns work you already did into drafts so the blank page stops being the reason you go quiet after two posts.
nodes.reading: Depth. Write one content-system doc with an audience of one, triggers, five questions, and a voice gate, then leave at least three dated drafts from a week of real work. Publishing comes later.
nodes.reviewFor: The doc is runnable next week without inventing a new process. Triggers and questions are explicit. Three dated drafts exist from real work, not recycled tips.

tasks.title: Write the content system doc
tasks.done_when: The doc names your audience of one, your triggers, the questions that produce a draft, and a short voice gate.
how: Keep it boring. Five questions beat a complex automation. Notion, Google Doc, or a gist are fine.

tasks.title: Run it for one week of drafts
tasks.done_when: At least three dated drafts sit in the same doc, each tied to a trigger from real work.
how: Drafts can stay unpublished. Prefer mission, review, or failure-log material over tips you read.

tasks.title: Save the doc URL
tasks.done_when: A stranger with the link can read the system and the drafts.
how: Gist, Notion public page, or Google Doc with link sharing on.

proves.claim: You can run a small system that turns work you already did into drafts, so going quiet is no longer the default.
proves.challenge: Write the content system doc and run it for one week.
proves.evidence: The doc URL with prompts and three dated drafts from real work.
proves.falsification: Drafts that are recycled tips; a process you could not run again next week; triggers left implicit.
proves.threshold: Runnable next week without inventing a process; explicit triggers; three real dated drafts.
proves.transfer: One post from the system and Two posts in seven days run on this; Research you ran yourself feeds it.

nodes.title: Swap the parser, keep the graph
nodes.evidence: your same queries running on the world server's C#: the map you make of it goes into your next world ticket.
nodes.why: The graph never knew who parsed it. That seam is the deepest lesson in the series, and the moment your tool and the game connect: you map the live world with the thing you built.
nodes.reading: Module 08. tree-sitter behind the same interface; then map the world server.
nodes.reviewFor: The same graph interface, a second language, and a blast radius on the world server.

tasks.title: tree-sitter behind the same interface
tasks.done_when: graph.json builds from a non-Python repo with zero changes to the query code.
how: The parser is a plugin; the graph is the contract.

tasks.title: Map the world server
tasks.done_when: Blast radius of the function your next world ticket touches, posted in #world.
how: This artifact feeds wd.ticket's map-before-you-touch task.

proves.claim: Your graph never knew who parsed it: you can swap the parser and map a second language with the same queries.
proves.challenge: Put tree-sitter behind the same interface and map the world server's C#.
proves.evidence: Your queries running on the world server; the map feeding your next ticket.
proves.falsification: A second graph type instead of a second parser; the world unmapped; queries that changed.
proves.threshold: Same interface, second language, a blast radius on the world server.
proves.transfer: Map before you touch, with your own tool, from here on.

nodes.title: One post from the system
nodes.evidence: A public post URL about real work, drafted from your content system.
nodes.why: One public post about work you can defend, with a link a stranger can open, is the moment the engine starts working outside the doc.
nodes.reading: Depth. Take one engine draft, tighten it until it is specific and linked to a receipt, then publish. Copied tips do not count.
nodes.reviewFor: Came from the engine doc. About your work, not a recycled tip. At least one concrete fact only you could claim. Links a PR, site page, or other receipt. Sounds like you. Still live.

tasks.title: Pick one engine draft and tighten it
tasks.done_when: One draft from the engine doc names the work, states X instead of Y because Z, and includes at least one concrete fact (system, failure, check, or link).
how: Run the voice gate from A system that feeds posts. Cut throat clearing. Keep what only you could write.

tasks.title: Publish with a receipt link
tasks.done_when: A public post is live, points at real work, and includes a link to your site page, PR, or other receipt.
how: LinkedIn is fine. A public post on your site counts. Prefer a short visual if you have one.

tasks.title: Save the post URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the live post.
how: Submit the public URL. Do not unpublish after review.

proves.claim: You can publish one post about work you can defend, with a receipt a stranger can open.
proves.challenge: Tighten one engine draft and publish it with a link.
proves.evidence: The live post URL.
proves.falsification: A recycled tip; no fact only you could claim; no receipt link.
proves.threshold: From the engine, about your work, one concrete fact, one receipt link, still live.
proves.transfer: Two posts in seven days; every post after; the research post.

nodes.title: One article you own
nodes.evidence: A public article URL on a topic you can defend, useful to other builders or agents.
nodes.why: An article is longer proof that you can teach a corner of the craft clearly enough that a serious reader can see how you think.
nodes.reading: Depth. Publish one article tied to mission work, with a point of view and at least one concrete example from your work. Prefer your site, then point LinkedIn at it.
nodes.reviewFor: Public URL. Clear point of view. At least one concrete example from your work with a link. Useful to another builder. Sounds like you. You could defend it aloud.

tasks.title: Pick the corner and the claim
tasks.done_when: A short note names the topic, the audience of one, the claim you will defend, and the receipt you will cite.
how: Prefer something from the mission: verification, review, a failure, a tradeoff. Not What is Git.

tasks.title: Publish one article
tasks.done_when: A public URL holds the full article with a point of view and at least one concrete example from your work.
how: Prefer your site. A gist series or known writing host is fine if the URL is public and stable. Cite your own receipts.

tasks.title: Point the trail at the article
tasks.done_when: Your site and LinkedIn (Featured, About, or a post) link the article so a stranger can find it from surfaces they already use.
how: Social is the pointer. The article is the home for the thinking.

tasks.title: Save the article URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the article.
how: Submit the public article URL.

proves.claim: You can teach a corner of the craft clearly enough that a serious reader sees how you think.
proves.challenge: Publish one article with a point of view and one concrete example from your work.
proves.evidence: The public article URL.
proves.falsification: No claim; no example from your work; a piece you could not defend aloud.
proves.threshold: Public, a clear point of view, one linked example, useful to another builder.
proves.transfer: Research you ran yourself is this shape with a method and numbers.

nodes.title: Research you ran yourself
nodes.evidence: A public research post on your site: a claim stated as a sentence that could be wrong, a method precise enough to repeat, the result with numbers including the disappointing ones, what it does not show, and what you would try next.
nodes.why: The skills this industry will hire for in three years do not have names yet. The people found for them were visibly testing them before the names arrived.
nodes.reading: Read The portfolio thread (disciplines 11), the research section, and Product and value engineering (disciplines 08) on causation. Small and honest beats large and vague: twelve tasks each way with a count is a research post.
nodes.reviewFor: a falsifiable claim, a method another engineer could repeat, real numbers, and limits stated before a reader states them.

tasks.title: Write the claim and the method
tasks.done_when: One sentence that could be wrong, and a method a stranger could run from your description without asking you.
how: Good shapes: does giving an agent the call graph reduce interventions on a mechanical refactor; does a cheaper model match a frontier one on a defined task class; does one check style catch a defect class the other misses.
If the claim cannot be wrong, it is an opinion, and this step does not accept opinions.

tasks.title: Run it
tasks.done_when: The method was executed as written, and the raw results are recorded before you interpret them.
how: Write the numbers down before you decide what they mean. Interpretation after recording, never during.

tasks.title: Publish with the numbers
tasks.done_when: Claim, method, result, what it does not show, next: five sections on your site, in your design system, with the numbers in the result.
how: State the limits before a reader does. That sentence is where a serious reader decides you can be trusted.

tasks.title: Save the post URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the post from a private window.
how: Point LinkedIn at it after it exists, not before.

video.title: A claim that could be wrong

proves.claim: You can run a small honest experiment and publish it in a form another engineer can repeat and check.
proves.challenge: Pick a claim you want the answer to; run a repeatable method; publish result and limits.
proves.evidence: The research post URL on your site.
proves.falsification: A claim that cannot be wrong; a method nobody could repeat; a result with no numbers; limits missing.
proves.threshold: All five sections present and specific, numbers in the result, limits stated.
proves.transfer: The method and causation sections of A number moved and Real people used it. Any later post from your content system.

nodes.title: Something others can use
nodes.evidence: A public repo or merged open-source PR that another person or agent could run or reuse.
nodes.why: A stranger who can try your work without you in the room is stronger proof than another private experiment, whether that work is a small tool or a merged PR.
nodes.reading: Depth. Ship a public repo or a merged PR another person could run or reuse, name who it helps, and document how to try it. Tutorial clones and typo-farm PRs do not count.
nodes.reviewFor: Public URL. Who it helps is clear. A stranger can clone the repo or open the PR and see what it is for, with enough docs to try. Not a tutorial dump. You can defend the change.

tasks.title: Choose the useful thing and who it helps
tasks.done_when: A short note names the artifact (own tool or upstream PR), who it helps, and how a stranger will try it.
how: Prefer a problem you hit on the mission or a tool you already use. Small and real beats famous and empty.

tasks.title: Publish or merge something useful
tasks.done_when: The artifact is public. README or PR description states what it does, who it helps, and how to try it.
how: New repo, or a merged PR on an existing project. A harness, script, dataset, docs fix that removes real confusion, or a bugfix all count if a stranger can use the result.

tasks.title: Run the stranger test
tasks.done_when: From a clean clone or the public PR page, you followed your own docs and reached a working try path without tribal knowledge.
how: If the docs fail, fix them before evidence. Link the work from your site project page when you can.

tasks.title: Save the repo or PR URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the public work.
how: Submit the repo or merged PR URL.

proves.claim: A stranger can try something you made without you in the room.
proves.challenge: Publish a small tool or merge an open-source PR, then run the stranger test.
proves.evidence: The public repo or merged PR URL.
proves.falsification: A tutorial dump; no clear beneficiary; a repo a stranger cannot run from the README.
proves.threshold: Public, who it helps is clear, a stranger can clone or open it and try, you can defend the change.
proves.transfer: Someone else can use it applies the same stranger test to your own system.

nodes.title: A number moved
nodes.evidence: A public outcome note: one metric in the world with a recorded baseline, the ranked hypotheses, the intervention you shipped, the number after, and how confident you are that you caused it and why. Or the evidence-backed case for not building it.
nodes.why: Correct code that changed nothing for anyone is a cost. This step asks the question every other step stops short of: did it matter, and can you show it.
nodes.reading: Read Product and value engineering (disciplines 08). Pick a metric the world already exposes or can with one counter: first-session length, players who return, chat messages in the first ten minutes. Record it before you touch anything. No baseline, no claim.
nodes.reviewFor: a baseline recorded before the change, hypotheses ranked by effect over cost, the smallest intervention, the number after, and an honest sentence on causation that names the mechanism, holdout or window used.

tasks.title: Pick the metric and record the baseline
tasks.done_when: The number is visible for several days before your change, with the event or query that produces it linked.
how: A counter and a weekly total is enough. The habit is what matters: before you claim success, know what number you would look at tomorrow to learn you were wrong.

tasks.title: Hypotheses, ranked by effect over cost
tasks.done_when: At least four hypotheses for why the number is not higher, each with confidence, plausible effect and cost of the smallest test, ranked, with one line on why the others waited.
how: 'We did not get to it' and 'we decided against it' are different sentences. Write the second.

tasks.title: Ship the smallest intervention
tasks.done_when: The change is live through the promote path, with the metric still recording.
how: Full ceremony: contract, PR, check, review. The intervention is a ticket like any other; what is different is the number waiting on the other side.

tasks.title: Measure and say how sure you are
tasks.done_when: Before and after in one table; the mechanism, holdout or window you used named; a confidence sentence a serious engineer would accept.
how: 'Retention rose nine points; no holdout; the intermediate measure also moved; moderate confidence we caused it' is the shape. 'We increased retention by fifty percent' is not.
If the number did not move, say so and say what you learned. That passes.

tasks.title: Save the outcome note
tasks.done_when: One public URL with baseline, ranking, intervention, result and the causation sentence.
how: Link the PR and the deploy note from it.

video.title: Retention is a number you can move

proves.claim: You can connect a technical change to an outcome someone experienced, and say how sure you are that you caused it.
proves.challenge: Own one metric in a live world from baseline through intervention to measurement.
proves.evidence: The outcome note at a public URL, linking the PR and deploy note.
proves.falsification: No baseline before the change; a causal claim with no mechanism, holdout or window; a percentage with no denominator.
proves.threshold: Baseline, ranked hypotheses, intervention, result, and a calibrated causation sentence; or an evidence-backed decision not to build.
proves.transfer: Every change to your own system in Real people used it. The value line in your defense.

nodes.title: Feed the model less, get more
nodes.evidence: a measured table: whole-file paste vs graph slice, tokens spent, answer quality, on three real questions.
nodes.why: Tokenomics as engineering instead of vibes. The graph computes the minimal context for a question; you measure what that is worth in money and accuracy.
nodes.reading: Module 09. Same doctrine as routing training, taught from the other side.
nodes.reviewFor: A measured pack: tokens and answer quality, whole-file paste versus graph slice.

tasks.title: nanograph pack --budget
tasks.done_when: Given a question and a token budget, the tool assembles the slice and the prompt.
how: Blast radius picks candidates; the budget trims them.

tasks.title: Measure it honestly
tasks.done_when: A committed table (or gist) in your nanograph repo includes at least one case where the slice LOST, plus why.
how: A benchmark with no losses is marketing, not measurement.
Done when the table lives in the repo or a stranger-openable URL, not only in chat.

proves.claim: You can compute the minimal context for a question and say, with numbers, what it is worth.
proves.challenge: Pack with a budget; measure whole-file paste against graph slice on three real questions.
proves.evidence: A measured table: tokens, answer quality, both ways, three questions.
proves.falsification: No measurement; one question; quality judged after seeing which was which.
proves.threshold: Three questions, both ways, tokens and quality recorded honestly.
proves.transfer: Context per task in You ran the agents; the cost line on every later PR.

nodes.title: Real people used it
nodes.evidence: A public note: five or more real users, a recorded baseline, one change chosen from evidence, the measured result with an honest causation sentence, the failures you documented, and one review by someone who owes you nothing.
nodes.why: Observed value is the proof revenue can only hint at. Five real people, a baseline, a change, a number: that is a receipt a stranger believes, and it is where a system that helps others starts to find them.
nodes.reading: Read Product and value engineering (disciplines 08). Revenue is not required and is deliberately not rewarded here; observed value is. If value turns into customers, the same baseline-and-result is the receipt, and it goes on the project page next to the PRs.
nodes.reviewFor: five counted users who are not you, a baseline before the change, the change chosen from evidence rather than preference, a result with a calibrated causation sentence, documented failures, and one outside review.

tasks.title: Find five users and record the baseline
tasks.done_when: Five people outside the cohort have used the system, their sessions are in the telemetry, and one metric that matters to them has a recorded baseline.
how: Ask people who have the problem, not people who like you. Friends count only if they actually have the problem.

tasks.title: Choose one change from evidence and ship it
tasks.done_when: The change is chosen from what the telemetry and the users showed, ranked against alternatives, shipped through your own evaluation harness, and live.
how: Write the ranking down. 'We decided against it' beats 'we did not get to it'.

tasks.title: Measure, document failures, get an outside review
tasks.done_when: Before and after in one table with a causation sentence; the failures the system had, written down; one engineer who did not help you has reviewed the note and their comments are attached.
how: The failures section is not optional and it is not a confession. It is what makes the rest believable.

tasks.title: Save the users note
tasks.done_when: One public URL with users, baseline, change, result, failures and the outside review.
how: This belongs on the project page on your site, in your design system.

proves.claim: You can put a system you own in front of real people and produce measured, independently reviewed evidence that a change improved something for them.
proves.challenge: Five users, baseline, evidence-chosen intervention, result, documented failures, outside review.
proves.evidence: The users note at a public URL.
proves.falsification: No baseline; users who are you under other names; a result with no denominator or no causation sentence; no failures listed; no outside review.
proves.threshold: All six elements present; the causation sentence names its method and its confidence.
proves.transfer: The value line on your project page and in your defense. The shape of every product claim you make afterward.

nodes.title: You defend it live
nodes.evidence: An unlisted recording of your defense, plus the filled external-reader form.
nodes.why: Eight minutes on camera defending your strongest change so far, to an engineer who did not help you. This is the strongest single artifact the program produces.
nodes.reading: Pick your strongest merged PR; the defense walks that one. The six defense questions and the external-reader form are pinned in Discord and in the repo's evidence folder. Read both before you record; there are no surprise questions.
nodes.reviewFor: you own the change live. The recording and the external form are both at the link.

tasks.title: Record the eight minutes
tasks.done_when: You answer the six defense questions without inventing detail.
how: Record unlisted. Answer the six defense questions without inventing detail you cannot show.

tasks.title: Two minutes on your own tools
tasks.done_when: In the recording you explain, in two minutes and without notes, what your graph tool and your modeled system do, one thing each taught you, and what an agent got wrong that you caught. A hiring manager could repeat it back.

tasks.title: Get one external verdict
tasks.done_when: A working engineer who did not help you filled the form.
how: The external-reader form is pinned in Discord next to the six questions.

tasks.title: Save recording and form
tasks.done_when: One URL that opens both, or two URLs in one note.
how: Submit it.

proves.claim: Your model of your own change survives contact with an engineer who did not help you, and it updates when a fact changes.
proves.challenge: Eight minutes on camera, six questions, one changed fact, two minutes on your own tools, no assistant in the room.
proves.evidence: The unlisted recording and the filled external-reader form.
proves.falsification: Confident fiction; a model that does not move when a fact changes; 'I know' where the honest word was 'I suspect'.
proves.threshold: External reader answers yes to the interview question; the changed-fact answer shows the model moving; the two minutes on your tools are specific enough to repeat.
proves.transfer: Every systems interview and incident review you will ever sit in; the defense of your own system if you build one.

nodes.title: Two posts in seven days
nodes.evidence: Two public post URLs published within the same seven-day window.
nodes.why: Two posts inside seven days prove the engine can run without waiting for a heroic mood.
nodes.reading: Depth. Publish two posts in one seven-day window that each meet the One post from the system bar: your work, a concrete fact, and a receipt link. Founding bar is two, not daily.
nodes.reviewFor: Two public posts dated inside the same seven days. Both from the engine, about real work, with receipts. Not two recycled tips.

tasks.title: Stage two engine drafts for the week
tasks.done_when: The engine doc names two drafts you will publish, each tied to a different trigger or piece of work, both ready to pass the One post from the system bar (receipt + concrete fact + your work).
how: If you only have one strong draft, run the questions on a second ship, review, or failure. Do not invent a tip post to fill the slot.

tasks.title: Publish two posts in seven days
tasks.done_when: Two live posts sit inside one seven-day window, each linking real work.
how: Same voice gate and receipt rule as One post from the system. Space them across the week if you can; do not dump both in one hour to game the clock.

tasks.title: Save both URLs with dates
tasks.done_when: One note lists both public URLs and the dates they went live.
how: Gist or doc with the two links and dates.

proves.claim: The engine runs without a heroic mood.
proves.challenge: Publish two engine posts inside seven days.
proves.evidence: Two public post URLs with dates.
proves.falsification: Two posts eight days apart; recycled tips; posts not from the engine.
proves.threshold: Two dated posts inside seven days, both from the engine, both with receipts.
proves.transfer: The cadence you keep after the cohort ends.

nodes.title: A stranger can find the work
nodes.evidence: One profile line or post that links your defense recording (or the merged PRs it stands on), published only after that receipt exists.
nodes.why: After the defense, one clear trail from LinkedIn to that receipt is how a hiring manager, a referral, or someone who Googled your name reaches the proof.
nodes.reading: Publish one LinkedIn post or one Featured / About line that points at the defense recording or the PR pack, only after that receipt exists, then walk the path in a private window.
nodes.reviewFor: A stranger can go from LinkedIn to the defense or its PR pack in under about ten seconds. The trail went up after the receipt existed. LinkedIn and the site tell the same story. No empty announcement.

tasks.title: Publish one trail to the defense
tasks.done_when: A live LinkedIn post or Featured / About line includes a clickable URL to the defense recording or the PR pack the defense walks.
how: One trail is the whole founding scope. Plain language. The work carries the persuasion.

tasks.title: Walk the stranger path
tasks.done_when: In a private window you opened public LinkedIn, followed the trail, and reached the defense or PR without hunting. Site project page still points at the same work if you have it.
how: If the click dies, fix links before evidence.

tasks.title: Save that trail URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the post or the live profile surface that points at the defense or that PR.
how: Submit the public URL once the path works.

proves.claim: A stranger who finds you on LinkedIn can reach your defense or its PR pack in seconds.
proves.challenge: Publish one trail that points at the defense receipt, after it exists, and walk it in a private window.
proves.evidence: The trail URL.
proves.falsification: A trail published before the receipt existed; an announcement with no link; LinkedIn and the site telling different stories.
proves.threshold: LinkedIn to the receipt in about ten seconds, published after the receipt, same story both places.
proves.transfer: Every future receipt gets the same trail; the habit is the credential.

nodes.title: Make it yours
nodes.evidence: your shipped fork: README with real numbers from a repo you care about, plus one analysis nobody asked for.
nodes.why: The finale is a fork, not a finish. This is the portfolio artifact that keeps working for you after the cohort, and the thing your defense can draw on.
nodes.reading: Modules 10-11. Full ceremony: contract, failure log, written review.
nodes.reviewFor: A shipped fork plus one analysis that exists only because you wanted the answer.

tasks.title: Ship the fork
tasks.done_when: A stranger can install it, run it on their repo, and read your numbers in the README.
how: Packaging is respect for the reader. Module 10.

tasks.title: One analysis nobody asked for
tasks.done_when: A query or view that exists because YOU wanted it, defended in one paragraph.
how: This is the part that gets reviewed hardest.

proves.claim: You own a tool that keeps working for you after the cohort, and you have used it to answer a question nobody asked.
proves.challenge: Ship the fork with real numbers; run one analysis because you wanted to.
proves.evidence: The shipped fork's README and the analysis.
proves.falsification: A fork with example output only; an analysis someone assigned.
proves.threshold: Real numbers from a repo you care about; one unassigned analysis.
proves.transfer: Research you ran yourself is this analysis published as a claim with a method.

nodes.title: A feature wearing your mark
nodes.evidence: your feature visible at play.gridschool.org with its maker's mark, and the PR that shipped it.
nodes.why: Anyone can say they built something. Your friends and family can walk into this one.
nodes.reading: Maker's marks are the only in-world credit. The world renders no progress bars: the thing itself is the proof.
nodes.coming: Opens when the web client is published at play.gridschool.org. The server-side path (ticket, deploy) is live now.

tasks.title: Ship a visible feature
tasks.done_when: A stranger at play.gridschool.org can see or use it without being told where to look.
how: Feature issues (GF-F1, GF-F2) or an earned proposal.

proves.claim: You shipped something visible in a live world that carries your mark.
proves.challenge: Ship a visible feature through the full path.
proves.evidence: The feature at play.gridschool.org and the PR that shipped it.
proves.falsification: A feature only visible locally; a mark with no PR behind it.
proves.threshold: Visible on the live domain with the PR linked.
proves.transfer: The project page on your site.

weekly.title: Ship one thing with a URL
weekly.done_when: A link posted in #ship from the last seven days.

weekly.title: One Coach session
weekly.done_when: You saved the review block and pasted it into #asks.
